Q5365.L1t: Pet food brands in the United States use memorable advertising slogans and jingles to market their products to cat owners.
Q5365.L2t: The slogan about cats asking for a food by name is part of a long-running advertising campaign that features a catchy jingle.
Q5365.L3t: The brand whose jingle is sung by cats repeating its own two-word name, with the line that cats 'ask for it by name,' is the one built on a meowing-sound name.
Q5365.L4t: The brand that claims cats ask for it by name is the one whose name is a pair of words imitating a cat's meow.
Q5365.L2f: The 'ask for it by name' slogan was first introduced in the 1920s as part of a radio campaign for a canned fish product.
Q5365.L3f: The 'cats ask for it by name' claim belongs to the premium gourmet line that is marketed with elegant, upscale imagery and the word 'Feast' in its title.
Q5365.L4f: The brand that claims cats ask for it by name is Fancy Feast.

Q5672.L1t: Criminal law recognizes that a person who assists or commands another to commit a crime can be held liable as an accomplice or principal.
Q5672.L2t: Under the common law, an accessory's liability was traditionally derivative of the principal's guilt, though modern rules often allow trying the accessory separately.
Q5672.L3t: A defense based on the principal's personal incapacity or mental condition does not negate the crime itself, whereas a finding that the shooting was justified means no crime was committed at all, leaving nothing for the instigator to be liable for.
Q5672.L4t: The defendant can assert a valid defense if the man was acquitted because the killing was justified as protecting himself from the victim.
Q5672.L2f: At common law, an accessory before the fact could never be tried unless the principal had first been convicted of the same offense.
Q5672.L3f: An acquittal grounded on the principal's lack of mental capacity means the killing itself was lawful, so no crime was committed by anyone and the instigator cannot be liable.
Q5672.L4f: The defendant will be able to assert a valid defense if the man's acquittal was based on insanity.

Q5969.L1t: Homicide law distinguishes among murder, manslaughter, and non-criminal killings based on the defendant's mental state and conduct.
Q5969.L2t: The felony murder rule can make a death during a felony murder, and its reach includes the period of flight until the felon reaches a place of temporary safety.
Q5969.L3t: Here the robbery was complete and the defendant had reached the safety of his hideout area an hour later, and the child darted out suddenly while he braked, so there was neither a killing in the felony's course nor criminal negligence or recklessness.
Q5969.L4t: The defendant should not be found guilty of any crime for the child's death because it was an unavoidable accident.
Q5969.L2f: Involuntary manslaughter requires only that the death be caused by the defendant's act, with no need to show negligence or recklessness.
Q5969.L3f: Because the defendant was driving away from a robbery with stolen money and tequila, he was driving with a reckless disregard for others, so the death resulted from his own criminal negligence.
Q5969.L4f: The defendant should be found guilty of involuntary manslaughter for the child's death.
